sections.title: Objective type questions (2 parts of 1 mark, or 4 parts of ½ mark).

questions.q: Complete the sentences: (I) Indian soldiers in the East India Company's army were not given promotion above that of ____. (II) A sepoy called ____ was the first soldier who openly disobeyed British orders.
questions.answer: (I) subedar (II) Mangal Pandey

questions.answer: Nana Saheb; Tantya Tope

questions.answer: (a) Birsa Munda (b) The Chhotanagpur Tenancy Act

questions.q: True or False: (a) The Revolt of 1857 spread equally to all parts of India, including Punjab and the Madras Presidency. (b) The Indigo Rebellion forced the government to declare compulsory indigo cultivation illegal in 1860.
questions.answer: (a) False — it was confined mainly to North and Central India. (b) True

questions.answer: (a) – (iii) Jhansi; (b) – (iv) Bareilly; (c) – (i) Delhi; (d) – (ii) Syed Ahmed Barelvi

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Explain any two reasons for the growing discontent among farmers growing indigo during British rule.
questions.answer: (1) They were paid very low prices for growing indigo; (2) Indigo was not lucrative as it was planted at the same time as food crops; And loss of fertility of the soil because of planting indigo.

or.q: Name the leader of the Wahabi movement and explain the significance of the movement.
or.answer: (1) (iv) Wahabi Movement (1830’s-1860’s): The leader of the movement was Syed Ahmed Barelvi of Rae Bareilly who was greatly influenced by the teachings of Abdul Wahab of Arabia and Shah Waliullah, a Delhi saint. (2) The movement was primarily religious in its origin. Irrespective of communal distinctions, peasants united against their landlords. The new class of zamindars that were created by the British became their political allies. All these factors helped to spread an anti-British feeling which ultimately culminated in the revolt of 1857.

questions.q: Describe the Jaintia and Garo Rebellion in brief.
questions.answer: (1) (iii) Jaintia and Garo Rebellion Rebellion (1860-1870s): After the First Anglo- Burmese War, the British planned the construction of a road connecting Brahmaputra Valley (present day Assam) with Sylhet (present day Bangladesh). (2) The Jaintias and the Garos in the North-Eastern part of India (present day Meghalaya) opposed the construction of this road which was of strategic importance to the British for the movement of troops. Alarmed, the British burnt several Jaintias and Garo villages. The hostilities increased with the introduction of House Tax and Income Tax by the British in 1860’s. (3) Jaintias leader U Kiang Nongbah was captured and publicly hanged and the Garo leader Pa Togan Sangma was defeated by the British.

questions.q: Explain one social and one religious cause of the Revolt of 1857.
questions.answer: Social: reforms such as the ban on sati, widow remarriage and women's education were seen as interference in Indian customs, and Indians were treated with contempt. Religious: missionary schools and Act XXI of 1850 (which let converts inherit property) made people fear forced conversion; sepoys feared losing caste by crossing the sea.

questions.q: List two grievances of the Indian sepoys against the British.
questions.answer: (1) They were paid less than English soldiers, could not rise above subedar and were often denied bhatta for overseas service. (2) The religious sentiments of the sepoys were hurt in 1806 in the Madras presidency. The Hindus were asked to remove their caste marks from their foreheads and the Muslims were asked to trim their beards. by certain military reforms which required them to serve overseas. The greased cartridges incident was the immediate cause of the revolt.

questions.q: Why is the Revolt of 1857 called the first national struggle for independence?
questions.answer: (1) Though begun by the sepoys, it was joined by peasants, artisans and others, and people of many regions fought together against the British. (2) They entered the Red Fort and proclaimed the aged and powerless Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar, as the Emperor of India. They declared the Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah as the emperor of India. Even though they failed to achieve their objective they succeeded in sowing the seeds of nationalism among the Indians. By now the British had become distrustful of the Hindu Muslim unity.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Explain the causes of the early resistance movements against British rule in India before the Revolt of 1857.
questions.answer: (1) British rule whose policies had undermined rights, status and economic position of Indians symbolised this exploitation. In Madras Presidency, Poligars rebelled, when the British tried to snatch away their military and land rights. For example, displaced zamindars and rulers wanted to regain their land and estates. (2) Heavy pressure was put on the zamindars and peasants to pay high taxes and grow commercial crops. revenue demand led to a large number of peasants losing their land to revenue farmers, traders and moneylenders. (3) Another group of people who revolted against the British rule were the tribals. The land and forests were their main source of livelihood. (4) Interference in religious practices angered people. They aimed to restore old structures and resist outside interference.

or.q: Explain the causes of the revolt of the Poligars of Madras.
or.answer: (1) In Madras Presidency, Poligars rebelled, when the British tried to snatch away their military and land rights. These rebellions were, however, local in character and effects. (v) The Kol Uprising (1831-1832): The Kols of Singhbhum in the Chhotanagpur area enjoyed autonomy under their chiefs but the entry of the British threatened their independence. (2) When the British tried to take away these rights, disband their armed retainers and collect revenue directly, they lost their power and income, so they rebelled; the British crushed them.

questions.q: Describe the Faqir and Sanyasi Rebellions of 1770–1820s.
questions.answer: (1) But this land could be sold off if he failed to pay the revenue The Sanyasis rose in rebellion after the great famine of 1770 in Bengal which caused acute chaos and misery. (2) The Bengal famine of 1770 led peasants whose lands were confiscated, displaced zamindars, disbanded soldiers and poor to come together in a rebellion. The Faqirs were a group of wandering Muslim religious mendicants in Bengal. (3) Two famous Hindu leaders who supported them were Bhawani Pathak and a woman, Devi Choudhurani. They attacked English factories and seized their goods, cash, arms and ammunition. (4) The British crushed them by the early 19th century.

questions.q: Explain four reasons why the peasants revolted against British rule.
questions.answer: (1) High land revenue under the Permanent, Ryotwari and Mahalwari settlements. (2) These peasants often borrowed money from the moneylenders, who were also called mahajans. The new zamindars from the city had little or no interest in the land. Very soon they became bonded labourers and could serve only their creditors. (3) Forced cultivation of commercial crops like indigo at low prices, reducing food and causing famines. (4) Harassment by officials, zamindars and middlemen and no access to justice.

questions.q: Why did the Revolt of 1857 fail? Explain.
questions.answer: (1) There was no unity of purpose among the rebels. They fought to liberate only their own territories. With the escape of Nana Sahib and the death of Bahadur Shah Zafar came the end of Peshwaship and the Mughal rule. (2) Secondly, this rising was not widespread it remained confined to North and Central India. Even in the north, Kashmir, Punjab, Sind and Rajputana kept away from the rebels. The British managed to get the loyalty of the Madras and Bombay regiments and the Sikh states. (3) The Bengal famine of 1770 led peasants whose lands were confiscated, displaced zamindars, disbanded soldiers and poor to come together in a rebellion. Thirdly the leadership of the movement was weak. Indian leaders lacked organisation and planning. The major reasons for its failure were – its localised and unorganised nature, weak leadership and lack of weapons and finances. (4) Shortage of modern weapons and money, while the British had the telegraph and control of the sea.

questions.q: Explain the impact of the Revolt of 1857 on India.
questions.answer: (1) In August 1858 the British crown assumed control of India from the East India Company and in 1877 Queen Victoria was crowned empress of India. This brought to an end the rule of East India Company. (2) . (3) The army was reorganised with more Europeans and fewer Indians; Indian artillery was disbanded. (4) However, it was the beginning of distrust between Hindus and Muslims which the British later exploited to continue their rule in India. They decided to follow the policy of divide and rule the country. (5) These were states that were enjoying British protection but their rulers had died without leaving Before the policy of Doctrine of Lapse, the Indian ruler had a right to adopt an heir to his throne even if he was childless, but now they had to take prior consent from the British. The Indian rulers were assured of their rights to succession after adoption. (6) They gave a heroic fight to the British government. No national leader emerged to coordinate the movement and give it purpose and direction. Even though they failed to achieve their objective they succeeded in sowing the seeds of nationalism among the Indians. Indian people became more aware of the heroes, who sacrificed themselves in the Revolt.

questions.q: Describe the Munda Rebellion and its significance.
questions.answer: (1) The Mundas traditionally enjoyed certain rights as the original clearer of the forest which was not given to the other tribes. But this land system was getting destroyed in the hands of the merchants and moneylenders long before the coming of the British. These contractors needed people to work with them as indentured laborers. (2) (ii) Munda Rebellion (1899-1900): One of the most important and prominent rebellion which took place after 1857 was the Munda Rebellion. The most prominent leader of this rebellion was Birsa Munda who was more aware than the others as he had received some education from the Missionaries. He encouraged his tribe people to keep the tradition of worshipping of the sacred groves alive. He attacked Police Stations, Churches and missionaries. (3) Unfortunately the rebels were defeated and Munda died in prison soon after in 1900. The Chhotanagpur Tenancy Act of 1908 provided some land ownership rights to the people and banned bonded labour of the tribal.

questions.q: Describe the political, economic, social and military causes of the Revolt of 1857.
questions.answer: (1) In fact, it was an economic, political and social struggle against the British rule. (2) Their policy of annexation called Doctrine of Lapse and Subsidiary Alliance led to a number of independent kingdoms being annexed to the British Empire. In this way Lord Dalhousie annexed the Maratha States of Satara, Nagpur , Jhansi and several other minor kingdoms. On the death of Baji Rao II, the pension granted to him was abolished and the claim of his adopted son, Nana Saheb, to receive this pension was denied to him. (3) Since they worked against the interests of Indian trade and industry, Indian handicrafts completely collapsed. Thus, the British drained India of her wealth and her natural resources. (4) The Britishers also imposed heavy duties on Indian made goods. revenue demand led to a large number of peasants losing their land to revenue farmers, traders and moneylenders. The economic decline of peasantry and artisans was reflected in 12 major and numerous minor famines from 1770 to 1857. Economic, political, social, religious and military causes were responsible for the Revolt of 1857. (5) reforms and missionary activity and Act XXI of 1850 made people fear conversion. Military: (6) by certain military reforms which required them to serve overseas. Some sepoys wanted special bhatta/allowance if sent on oversea duty. They were paid salaries less than their English counterparts. (7) greased cartridges believed to contain cow and pig fat hurt both Hindus and Muslims.

questions.q: Explain the nature and significance of the Revolt of 1857.
questions.answer: (1) They began to march towards Delhi, where they were joined by the local infantry and the common people. The revolt was started by the sepoys but was joined in large numbers by the civilian population. The participation of peasants and artisans made the revolt a widespread and popular event. (2) The cow is sacred to the Hindus and the pig is forbidden to the Muslims. Talukdars and peasants in Awadh fought together against a common foe. of success against an organised and powerful enemy. (3) They were isolated from each other because each rebellion had a different motive. Called the Sepoy Mutiny by the British, it is now recognised as the First War of Independence against the British rulers. Rebels in one part of the country helped people fighting in other areas. (4) It took many years for the British to crush the Mappilas. This brought to an end the rule of East India Company. The crown promised to honor all the treaties and the agreements made by the company with the rulers of Indian State. The East India Company’s rule was abolished in 1858 through a declaration of the Queen’s Proclamation by the British Parliament. (5) The British policies proved harmful to the tribal society. They decided to follow the policy of divide and rule the country. The Army had been mainly responsible for the crisis of 1857. (6) It also provided the necessary foundation for the later successful anti-colonial struggles against the British. Even though they failed to achieve their objective they succeeded in sowing the seeds of nationalism among the Indians.
